newsitem.title: USA: Airlines offer half-price child air fare.
newsitem.headline: Airlines offer half-price child air fare.

text.p: American Airlines on Wednesday led major U.S. airlines in offering half-price fares for children under the age of two, a move aimed at encouraging parents to put their children in safety seats.

American, a unit of AMR Corp, announced the 50 percent discount on children's fares within the United States and Canada at a news conference -- complete with a row of airline seats and a 9-month-old infant.
The move was later matched by UAL Corp 's United Airlines, US Airways Group Inc., Delta Air Lines Inc. and Northwest Airlines Inc.

The airlines cited federal studies that children traveling in safety seats were safer than children held by an adult and predicted the lower fares would encourage passengers to travel with safety seats.
The fares apply for children under the age of 2 who occupy their own airplane seat, in a government-approved child safety seat. Adults must supply the seats.
"It is designed to encourage the use of child restraint safety seats," UAL spokesman Joe Hopkins said.
Formerly, parents would hold children under the age of 2 on their laps, a practice that has been found to be dangerous, an American Airlines official said.
US Airways said the discounts applied on most published fares, with two children permitted to travel per adult on the lower fares.

Federal rules still allow children under 2 years of age to travel free of charge when held by an adult, and the airline said it would continue its efforts to find an adjacent seat for non-ticketed infants whenever possible.

The National Transportation Safety Board welcomed the move. The board has repeatedly recommended that the Federal Aviation Administration require all babies to occupy a child safety seat, rather than allowing parents to hold their young children.
The FAA has refused thus far to order the move, partly because it would increase the cost of flying and divert some families to automobiles.
"The FAA has been unwilling to take that step, so I'm glad to see that awareness coming out of the airlines and American Airlines," NTSB Chairman Jim Hall told reporters.
